messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

When Sergeant‑Major Daniel Rossi, a 49‑year‑old council member in a midsize Midwestern city, first heard the shrapnel burst above the front yard of his family home, he was 25 and fighting in Iraq. The explosion ripped a hole in the sky, threw debris across the street, and left a half‑cannon shell embedded in a neighbor’s fence. In the heat of that moment, a patrol of men rushed to his side, and a sudden burst of gunfire cut his life in half, forcing him onto a stretcher that was later transported to a U.S. base in the desert. He remembers the smell of burning fuel, the crackling of his squad’s radios, the frantic hiss of the commander’s voice telling them to “hold position.” He never saw the entire picture; the rest of the day blurred into a haze of white‑noise and instinct. The memories that surface today are fragmented. Daniel speaks of “incomplete picture” and “terror on recall,” noting how a single flash of a shell’s detonation can send him spiraling back into that instant, his heart pounding and breathing shallow. The incomplete memory makes him doubt what he can narrate: he often stumbles when telling his wife or a friend about that day, losing the thread before the story reaches a logical ending. As those memories rise, Daniel automatically pulls out his coping tools: he slams the volume on the radio, his apartment’s TV, or a playlist of loud rock, allowing the roar of music to drown out the sharp sound of a gunshot in his mind. He also watches his thoughts as if they were strangers, constantly scanning for a sign that the panic he feels is a sign of “going crazy.” In the same breath, the memory pushes him to feel the world as hostile, his body as an enemy that remains on alert. These appraisals, in turn, sharpen the threat he perceives when he hears a sudden thud on a door or feels a hand brush his arm in the hallway—anything that feels like a touch that could be a weapon. After the war, the threat that had once been a concrete, external danger became a pervasive, internal sense of peril. Daniel tells himself that no one is truly safe, no matter how often his colleagues reassure him that the city is calm. He cannot trust the quiet after a meeting or the lull between council sessions. Even when the mayor’s office is full of polite smiles, the feeling of danger lingers. Sleep, too, has become elusive: he wakes to the hiss of wind through a cracked window and spends hours in a half‑awakened state, listening for the rumble of traffic that could be a convoy. In those nights, the threat feeds the memory, replaying fragments of that explosive day as a phantom echo in his mind, and the memory feeds the threat, convincing him that every ordinary sound could be a prelude to disaster. These two forces feed one another in a loop that Daniel recognizes only in hindsight. The coping strategies he relies on—sensory distraction, thought monitoring, and avoidance of touch—have become woven into the fabric of his daily life. When he steps onto the council podium, he positions himself slightly away from the audience, keeping his hands tucked in his lap so no one can touch him. He watches the hallway clock with a distance that feels like a buffer between him and the world, and when a colleague leans in for a hug, he automatically pulls back, citing the “need to stay safe.” These behaviors are not merely avoidance; they are attempts to keep his senses from being flooded by a threat that he feels is ever-present. Yet each time he suppresses a touch or diverts his attention to music, he also stokes the memory of that shrapnel burst, because the act of distraction reminds him that he is still in a state of fight or flight. In turn, the memory of that moment intensifies his negative appraisal of his own body: every ache or flutter in his chest is a reminder that his body remains a sentinel, always ready for an attack. Over the months, these patterns have begun to erode his relationships and his performance at work. The council’s new community outreach project required Daniel to attend several meetings where he was expected to engage with local businesses and residents, many of whom reached out with friendly touches or handshakes as a customary greeting. Instead, he avoided the interaction, and the repeated rejections piled up, turning a once‑promising partnership into a stalled initiative. His wife, noticing the growing distance between them, urged him to seek help. Daniel’s fear of the world being dangerous, his hypervigilance at every sound, and the terror that swallows him when he hears a door creak are the things that finally compel him to step into a therapist’s office. He hopes to untangle the memory that keeps pulling him back to that night in Iraq, to reclaim a sense of safety in his own body, and to learn a way to respond to others’ touches without feeling the sudden surge of danger that has haunted him for years.
